title: Collaboration
author: Nick Hart
summary: In the fourth post of a series on Richard Claydon's six sense-making disciplines, Nick Hart treats collaboration as the discipline that shapes how groups think together, not merely how they feel together. He argues that schools often assume collaboration exists because meetings are frequent, when frequent interaction does not guarantee expanded thinking. Collaboration must instead be produced by deliberate design of participation, and he sets out four strategies: getting the right people around the table, equal airtime, framing problems before solutions, and debriefing how decisions were made. Each strategy is explained in terms of the cognitive failure it prevents, such as dominant voices narrowing group thinking or premature convergence on the wrong problem. He concludes that these are structural habits rather than occasional facilitation techniques, designed to interrupt dominance and unexamined assumptions so that collective intelligence can exceed individual capability.
points: Hart distinguishes collaboration from meeting frequency, arguing that without deliberate structure sense making becomes narrow and dependent on dominant voices.
Equal airtime is defined as equal opportunity to shape understanding rather than equal influence, using round robins and invitations to quieter colleagues.
Framing the problem before proposing solutions guards against decisive-feeling answers that fail to resolve underlying tensions.
Short debriefs after major decisions, examining whose perspectives were absent, are presented as the way collective thinking improves across cycles of work.
The strategies are framed as standing structural habits that protect cognitive diversity, most needed when agreement arrives too quickly or dissent goes underground.
quotes: Collaboration shapes how groups think together, not just how they feel together. Without it, sense making becomes narrow, predictable and overly dependent on dominant voices.
In schools, collaboration is often assumed because meetings are frequent. Yet frequent interaction does not guarantee expanded thinking.

Collaboration is produced through deliberate design of participation, exercised repeatedly and made visible to others. In complex systems, leaders cannot assume collective intelligence will emerge automatically; they must structure for it.
Equal airtime does not mean equal influence; it means equal opportunity to shape understanding. When certain voices consistently lead, group thinking narrows. Others disengage or self censor.
When framing is weak, teams can focus on the wrong issues. Solutions feel decisive but fail to resolve underlying tension. Collaboration improves when interpretation precedes prescription.
Without debrief, patterns repeat unnoticed. With debrief, collective thinking improves incrementally. Debriefing stabilises learning across cycles of work.
They are not facilitation techniques to deploy occasionally; they are structural habits that protect cognitive diversity within teams. Their phrasing is intentionally direct.
